newsitem.title: AUSTRALIA: RTRS-Australian Broadcasting Corp Morning Update.
newsitem.headline: RTRS-Australian Broadcasting Corp Morning Update.

text.p: SURVEY SHOWS HIRING PLANS HAVE IMPROVED
There's good news for job seekers this morning - a survey by a national recruitment agency shows employers are looking to hire.
Of the three-thousand organisations surveyed by Morgan and Banks, only government agencies reported negative hiring intentions.
The number of employers planning to hire staff over the next three months has risen by four per cent since the last survey.
Head of economic research at Morgan and Banks, John Winter, says hiring intentions are positive in every state and territory except the A-C-T.
Mr Winter says the result in Western Australia was very positive, where nearly a third of employers are looking to hire.
PM SEES BRIGHT FUTURE FOR AUSTRALIA
The Prime Minister says he's as positive and optimisitic about Australia's future, as he is about its past.

Mr Howard was speaking at a business awards dinner last night, after warnings from his predecessor, Paul Keating, that the country's future was at risk because of the Government's failure to curb racism.

In a television hook-up to more than three thousand small business people nationwide, Mr Howard said he was confident Australia could make its own way in the world, despite the radical changes it's facing.
WA'S COURT CAGEY ABOUT PREMIERS MEETING

There's confusion over whether West Australian Premier Richard Court will attend this week's Council of Australian Governments meeting in Brisbane, as speculation grows over an early election announcement.
The meeting in Brisbane on Friday is expected to discuss tax reform with other conservative Premiers pressuring the Prime Minister over tax reform.
While John Howard has ruled out any major overhaul in his first term, there is a push for reform, including a goods and services tax, to be part of a Howard government's second term.
It's an issue Mr Court has embraced enthusiastically, repeatedly calling for a G-S-T to be part of the tax reform debate.
The COAG meeting, however, could coincide with the first day of an election campaign.
Last night, the Premier's office would not confirm if Mr Court would be attending the meeting, saying only that a ticket was booked.
It's understood a senior minister or adviser could represent Mr Court.
There is a precedent for such action, with former Queensland Premier Wayne Goss declining to attend one meeting when an election was called in that state.
ALICE TO DARWIN RAIL BID TO BE PUT TO PM
The leaders of the Northern Territory and South Australian governments will take an Alice Springs-to-Darwin railway project brief to the Prime Minister.
The Territory and South Australian governments sign an agreement today, aimed at furthering the project.
The agreement covers financial commitments, the establishment of the AustralAsia Railway Corporation, and the project brief.
Territory Railway Minister Barry Coulter says the two government leaders will seek a Commonwealth commitment to the railway, and its membership in the Corporation.
He says John Howard's support is vital, but ultimately, the market will determine if the project is viable.
ABC MUST CONSIDER MARDI GRAS CONCERNS

ABC Chairman, Donald McDonald, says he doesn't believe an approach to the ABC by Federal Communications Minister, Richard Alston, over the televising of the Gay and Lesbian Mardi Gras was done with any malice.
Senator Alston has said he was just drawing to the attention of the ABC concerns of people who've complained to his Department about the broadcast.
He's said all he did was inquire whether the ABC plans to end the broadcast or schedule it at a later time.
The ABC's chairman says he's heard similar concerns from Federal backbenchers who've had submissions from their constituents.
Mr McDonald says he doesn't know what has triggered the concerns, but the Minister's inquiries will have to be considered.
-- Reuters Sydney Newsroom 61-2 9373-1800
